summary: Defines a framework for coupling the Active Queue Management algorithms of two queues, for flows that respond to congestion differently. It offers a path for the Internet to move from classic Reno-friendly congestion control to scalable congestion control with very low queuing delay. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Two lines at a shop, one for gentle shoppers and one for pushy ones, are linked so both get a fair turn and the gentle line stays quick.

questions: how do l4s and classic traffic share a bottleneck
what is the coupling factor k in l4s
why does l4s use two queues
subtitle: Two linked queues let low-latency Scalable traffic and Classic TCP-style traffic share one link fairly without per-flow inspection.

tldr.problem: Classic congestion controls such as Reno and CUBIC need a big queue to keep a link full, which makes queuing delay vary. Scalable controls that could give consistently low delay were too aggressive to share an ECN-capable queue with them.
tldr.mechanism: A DualQ Coupled AQM keeps an L4S queue and a Classic queue. The Classic queue's drop probability is tied to the L4S marking probability by p_C = (p_CL / k)^2, so both kinds of flow get roughly the same throughput, while the L4S queue gets conditional priority for low delay.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental specification. It lets Scalable congestion controls be deployed on the shared Internet, without clean-slate environments such as private data centres.

facts.label: Required default configuration
facts.value: None needed on the public Internet (SHOULD NOT)

today: RFC 9332 is an Experimental RFC, published in January 2023, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with the L4S architecture in RFC 9330 and the L4S ECN protocol in RFC 9331.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
RFC 9332 specifies a framework for DualQ Coupled AQMs, which serve as the network part of the L4S architecture in RFC 9330. Latency is becoming the critical performance factor for many applications, and queuing remains a major intermittent part of it. The RFC argues that better AQMs in the network alone, or better congestion control in end systems alone, are both yielding diminishing returns.

The text reports that recent single-queue AQMs are tuned to let a typical Reno-friendly flow induce an average queue that roughly doubles the base round-trip time, adding 5-15 ms of queuing on average. It also gives 20-30 ms as the 99th percentile queuing delay with those AQMs, against 2 ms with L4S for the same traffic.

Until now, Scalable controls such as DCTCP did not coexist well with Classic ones in a shared ECN-capable queue, because Scalable controls are so aggressive that Classic flows drive themselves to a small capacity share. They could only be deployed where a clean-slate environment could be arranged.
sections.plainLanguage: Some internet programs need to wait in a long line to go fast, and others want almost no wait. When they shared one line, the pushy ones crowded out the rest. This document builds two linked lines so both kinds get what they need.

sections.title: Classic and Scalable Congestion Control
sections.content:
The Classic service is for congestion controls that coexist with Reno without hurting its flow rate, such as Reno itself and CUBIC. The L4S service is for Scalable congestion controls such as Prague, which was derived from Data Center TCP. With Classic controls, it now takes hundreds of round trips to recover after a congestion signal, so control of queuing and utilization becomes very slack.

A Scalable congestion control is one where the average time from one congestion signal to the next stays the same as flow rate scales. For instance, DCTCP averages 2 congestion signals per round trip, whatever the flow rate. Scalable controls make far smaller rate variations than Reno-friendly ones and shift smoothing from the network to the sender. Both changes only work with ECN signalling, not drop: with ECN, high marking levels are just signals, not impairments.

L4S packets are identified by the experimentally assigned ECN codepoints ECT(1) and CE in the IP header (see RFC 8311 and RFC 9331).
sections.plainLanguage: Pushy shoppers keep tiny, quick steps and ask the cashier for a nudge all the time. Careful shoppers take big slow steps and only react when something goes wrong. The two styles need different treatment.

sections.title: The Coupled AQM
sections.content:
To a first-order approximation, the steady-state congestion window of Reno is inversely proportional to the square root of the drop probability p. For DCTCP, the window is inversely proportional to p itself, where p is the ECN-marking probability. So for safe coexistence, the drop probability for Classic traffic (p_C) has to differ from the marking probability for L4S traffic (p_L). RFC 8311 updates the original ECN spec (RFC 3168), which required them to be the same, to allow experiments where they differ.

The Coupled AQM makes the Classic drop probability proportional to the square of the coupled L4S probability p_CL, so the squaring counterbalances the square root in the Reno formula. The constant of proportionality k is the coupling factor.

The Classic AQM is built in two stages: a base stage that outputs an internal probability p' (p-prime), then a squaring stage. The L queue also has a Native AQM that tracks the instantaneous L queue delay, and the marking applied to L traffic is the larger of that and the coupled value.
sections.plainLanguage: The slow line's waiting-time penalty is squared before it reaches the quick line, like a recipe that balances a big step on one side with a small step on the other, so both kinds of shopper end up with similar-sized portions.

sections.title: The Dual Queue Structure
sections.content:
A classifier on the left separates incoming traffic between the L and C queues. Each queue has its own AQM that decides the likelihood of marking or dropping (p_L and p_C). A scheduler then forwards packets to the link, giving the L queue conditional priority.

The priority has to be conditional so the C queue cannot be starved in the short term. If there is only a small finite set of C packets, such as a DNS request or an initial window of data, some Classic AQMs would not induce enough ECN marking in the L queue to make it yield. Coupling only runs in one direction, from Classic to L4S. Because the scheduler is work preserving, any C traffic is scheduled in gaps that responsive L flows leave when they slow down.

Operators may also steer other packets into the L queue by their own classifiers, so it can be seen as a general low-latency queue. The RFC gives two example algorithms in appendices: DualPI2, based on a Proportional Integral controller, and Curvy RED, derived from RED. Both regulate queues against targets in units of time rather than bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The quick line is allowed to go first, but only up to a point, so the slow line never waits forever. When the slow line gets long, it also tells the quick-line shoppers to ease off.

sections.title: What an Implementation Must Do
sections.content:
A DualQ Coupled AQM implementation MUST use two queues, each with an AQM algorithm, and the AQM for the L queue MUST be able to apply ECN marking. The scheduler MUST give L4S packets priority over Classic, but that priority MUST be bounded so Classic traffic is not starved. The scheduler SHOULD be work-conserving or close to it.

The AQM MUST apply ECN marking to L queue traffic that is no lower than what equation (1) derives from the likelihood of drop in the Classic queue. The value of k does not have to be standardised for interoperability, but a value of 2 is RECOMMENDED, and operators MAY choose another value. If the AQM detects overload, it MUST introduce Classic drop to both types of ECN-capable traffic until the overload episode has subsided.

By default, a DualQ Coupled AQM SHOULD NOT need any configuration for use at a bottleneck on the public Internet. The RFC lists parameters operators MAY configure, and says an experimental implementation SHOULD offer monitoring (such as bits forwarded and mean and 99th percentile queue delay per queue) and anomaly reporting (such as start time and duration of overload).
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: keep two lines, let the quick line go first but never forever, and if the shop gets overcrowded, turn people away from both lines. The shop should work without anyone fiddling with settings.

sections.title: Unresponsive Flows and Overload
sections.content:
The DualQ gives low delay without per-flow processing, so users who encrypt flow identifiers, for example in VPN tunnels, do not have to give up low delay. Per-flow rate policing or queue protection can be added as an optional module.

The basic goal is that unresponsive flows get no more throughput advantage than they would in a single-queue AQM. The RFC discusses two ways to keep Classic from short-term starvation: weighted round robin (sacrifice some L4S throughput, with a Classic weight such as 1/16) or a time-shifted FIFO (sacrifice some L4S delay).

When L4S ECN marking saturates, the RFC contrasts drop on saturation with delay on saturation. The example DualPI2 algorithm uses drop on saturation, which also limits the advantage unresponsive ECN-capable traffic would otherwise gain. The RFC says these policy choices belong to developers or operators rather than the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone ignores the shop rules and pushes in, the shop still treats them no better than in a single line. When it gets very crowded, the shop starts turning people away from both lines to restore order.
